claims.text: The initial alloy is equiatomic FeCoNiCrMn.
The initial alloy has a largely homogeneous, disordered microstructure.
Annealing equiatomic FeCoNiCrMn at approximately 750 °C for 20–60 minutes followed by rapid quenching will form a uniform distribution of nanoscale precipitates.
In situ TEM or XRD can be used during annealing to monitor and optimize precipitate formation.
Real-time microstructural monitoring is critical for obtaining consistent precipitate nucleation and growth without excessive coarsening.
Rapid quenching preserves the nanoscale precipitate distribution created during annealing.
The annealing treatment produces uniformly dispersed nanoscale secondary phases, such as ordered intermetallic or carbide precipitates, within the disordered matrix.
Uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates act as domain-wall pinning centers.
The precipitates hinder domain-wall motion during magnetization reversal.
Increased domain-wall pinning raises the coercive field relative to the baseline material.
The treated alloy will have a coercive field approximately 20–30% higher than that of an identical alloy processed without the precipitate-inducing heat treatment.
The coercivity enhancement should hold when annealing is performed near 750 °C in an inert atmosphere and is followed by rapid quenching.
Deviations in temperature or atmosphere may nullify the coercivity enhancement.
Insufficient control over precipitate formation may nullify the coercivity enhancement.
The magnitude of coercivity enhancement depends on precipitate size and spatial distribution.
